ABSTRACT
In modern manufacturing environments, factories rely heavily on automated machinery and complex systems to maintain high productivity and operational efficiency. However, machine failures such as overheating, electrical faults, and safety-related incidents can cause unexpected downtime, leading to production losses and increased maintenance costs. Traditionally, resolving such incidents depends heavily on experienced engineers, which can delay resolution and increase Mean Time to Repair (MTTR).
With advancements in Artificial Intelligence, Large Language Models (LLMs), and intelligent automation, it is now possible to design systems that assist operators in diagnosing and resolving machine-related issues in real time. The Intelligent Incident Resolution Assistant aims to leverage AI-driven agents, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and automated workflows to analyse machine incidents, suggest corrective actions, and notify relevant stakeholders efficiently.
To support such intelligent systems, robust data pipelines are essential. In manufacturing, vast amounts of heterogeneous data are generated from production lines, machines, and enterprise systems. A data pipeline collects this raw data (via IoT devices, SCADA, ERPs, etc.), cleans and transforms it, and delivers it to analytics or ML models. Effective ETL/ELT pipelines turn raw sensor and process data into actionable insights that drive operational efficiency. For instance, manufacturing industries “generate massive amounts of data,” and pipelines are needed to integrate and normalize this data for real-time monitoring and AI inference.
This project focuses on building an agent-based intelligent assistant that integrates with manufacturing systems to classify incidents, retrieve relevant knowledge from SOPs and maintenance records, and take appropriate actions such as guiding operators or escalating issues to maintenance teams.

OBJECTIVES
To design an AI-based assistant for intelligent incident resolution, capable of understanding, analysing, and responding to machine-related issues in a manufacturing environment with minimal human intervention.
To automatically classify machine incidents as mechanical, electrical, or safety-related, enabling appropriate prioritization and efficient handling of reported issues.
To retrieve relevant Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), maintenance manuals, and past incident records using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in order to provide accurate and context-aware information for decision-making.
To assist factory operators by providing clear, step-by-step resolution guidance, allowing them to safely resolve minor issues without immediate dependence on maintenance engineers.
To automate the creation and updating of maintenance tickets in the CMMS system, ensuring timely escalation of incidents that require expert intervention.
To notify relevant stakeholders through integrated communication platforms such as email and Teams/Slack, thereby ensuring effective coordination between operators, maintenance teams, and supervisors.
To reduce the Mean Time to Repair (MTTR) by enabling faster incident diagnosis, guided resolution, and automated escalation mechanisms.
To improve overall factory operational efficiency, by minimizing equipment downtime, reducing dependency on senior engineers, and streamlining incident management workflows.

1. INTRODUCTION
1.1 General Introduction to the topic
In modern manufacturing environments, factories rely heavily on automated machinery and
complex systems to maintain high productivity and operational efficiency. However, machine
failures such as overheating, electrical faults, and safety-related incidents can cause unexpected
downtime, leading to production losses and increased maintenance costs. Traditionally,
resolving such incidents depends heavily on experienced engineers, which can delay resolution
and increase Mean Time to Repair (MTTR).
With advancements in Artificial Intelligence, Large Language Models (LLMs), and intelligent
automation, it is now possible to design systems that assist operators in diagnosing and
resolving machine-related issues in real time. The Intelligent Incident Resolution Assistant
aims to leverage AI-driven agents, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and automated
workflows to analyse machine incidents, suggest corrective actions, and notify relevant
stakeholders efficiently.
This project focuses on building an agent-based intelligent assistant that integrates with
manufacturing systems to classify incidents, retrieve relevant knowledge from SOPs and
maintenance records, and take appropriate actions such as guiding operators or escalating
issues to maintenance teams.
1.2 Organisation
Dassault Systèmes is a French global software company specializing in 3D design, simulation,
product lifecycle management (PLM), and virtual twin solutions for industries such as
aerospace, automotive, and manufacturing. The company’s 3DEXPERIENCE platform
provides a unified environment for modelling, engineering, and operations. A key focus of
Dassault Systèmes is on “Virtual Twins” – scientific, data-driven digital models of real-world
products and production systems. These virtual twins integrate real-time data to simulate
behaviour, enabling enhanced process control and continuous optimization across the product
lifecycle. Dassault Systèmes has publicly described virtual twins as the “cornerstone of the
next industrial revolution,” combining modelling, simulation, and AI to drive smarter
manufacturing.
Within Dassault Systèmes, the NETVIBES team (part of the Information Intelligence brand)
delivers data analytics and AI-driven insights. NETVIBES provides a data science platform
that “transforms massive information flows into actionable insights” and “augments the virtual
twin experience with contextualized real-world data”. In practice, NETVIBES products allow
business and engineering users to visualize and analyse data from multiple sources (IoT, ERP,

maintenance logs, etc.) in dashboards and AI models. For example, Dassault Aviation (the
aircraft manufacturer) uses 3DEXPERIENCE NETVIBES to maximize fleet availability by
feeding operational data through NETVIBES’s data science portfolio. Another NETVIBES
solution called “AI-Maximized Asset Performance” applies machine learning and feedback
loops to optimize asset uptime across a fleet. In short, NETVIBES combines big data, AI/ML,
and Dassault’s virtual twin concepts to deliver manufacturing insights and automated decision
support. (Notably, Dassault Systèmes merged its EXALEAD data search technology into the
NETVIBES brand in 2021.)
1.3 Area of Computer Science
This project lies at the intersection of multiple domains within Computer Science, including:
i. Artificial Intelligence (AI) – for intelligent decision-making and automation
ii. Natural Language Processing (NLP) – for understanding operator-reported issues
and system logs
iii. Large Language Models (LLMs) – for reasoning, classification, and response
generation
iv. Multi-Agent Systems – for modular and scalable incident handling
v. Information Retrieval & RAG – for retrieving relevant SOPs, manuals, and historical
incidents
vi. Distributed Systems – for integrating MES, CMMS, notification platforms, and AI
services
The project demonstrates a real-world application of AI agents in industrial automation and
smart manufacturing.

2. NEED FOR THE PROJECT
Manufacturing industries face frequent machine-related incidents that require immediate
attention to prevent downtime. The current manual approach to incident resolution often
involves delays due to the unavailability of experienced personnel and lack of quick access to
historical data and SOPs.
The need for this project arises from:
i. Increasing complexity of manufacturing systems
ii. High dependency on senior engineers
iii. Slow response time to machine failures
iv. Lack of centralized knowledge access for operators
The Intelligent Incident Resolution Assistant addresses these challenges by providing real-
time, AI-driven support, enabling faster and more reliable incident resolution.
3. OBJECTIVES
i. To design an AI-based assistant for intelligent incident resolution, capable of
understanding, analysing, and responding to machine-related issues in a manufacturing
environment with minimal human intervention.
ii. To automatically classify machine incidents as mechanical, electrical, or safety-
related, enabling appropriate prioritization and efficient handling of reported issues.
iii. To retrieve relevant Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), maintenance
manuals, and past incident records using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
(RAG) in order to provide accurate and context-aware information for decision-
making.
iv. To assist factory operators by providing clear, step-by-step resolution guidance,
allowing them to safely resolve minor issues without immediate dependence on
maintenance engineers.

v. To automate the creation and updating of maintenance tickets in the CMMS
system, ensuring timely escalation of incidents that require expert intervention.
vi. To notify relevant stakeholders through integrated communication platforms such
as email and Teams/Slack, thereby ensuring effective coordination between operators,
maintenance teams, and supervisors.
vii. To reduce the Mean Time to Repair (MTTR) by enabling faster incident diagnosis,
guided resolution, and automated escalation mechanisms.
viii. To improve overall factory operational efficiency, by minimizing equipment
downtime, reducing dependency on senior engineers, and streamlining incident
management workflows.
4. METHODOLOGY
The project follows an agent-based architecture where each agent performs a specific task:
i. Issue Submission
- Operator submits an incident via text or voice input through MES.
ii. Incident Classification Agent
- Classifies the issue into mechanical, electrical, or safety categories using an
LLM.
iii. RAG Retrieval Agent
- Retrieves relevant documents from SOPs, past incidents, and maintenance
manuals using a vector database.
iv. Decision Logic Agent
- Determines whether the issue can be resolved by the operator or needs
maintenance escalation.
v. Action Agent
- Sends step-by-step guidance to operators
- Creates CMMS tickets if required
- Sends notifications via email and Teams/Slack
vi. Feedback and Logging
- Stores resolution outcomes for future learning and improvement
This modular approach ensures scalability, maintainability, and efficient handling of factory
incidents.

INTRODUCTION
General Introduction to the topic
In modern manufacturing environments, factories rely heavily on automated machinery and complex systems to maintain high productivity and operational efficiency. However, machine failures such as overheating, electrical faults, and safety-related incidents can cause unexpected downtime, leading to production losses and increased maintenance costs. Traditionally, resolving such incidents depends heavily on experienced engineers, which can delay resolution and increase Mean Time to Repair (MTTR).
With advancements in Artificial Intelligence, Large Language Models (LLMs), and intelligent automation, it is now possible to design systems that assist operators in diagnosing and resolving machine-related issues in real time. The Intelligent Incident Resolution Assistant aims to leverage AI-driven agents, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and automated workflows to analyse machine incidents, suggest corrective actions, and notify relevant stakeholders efficiently.
This project focuses on building an agent-based intelligent assistant that integrates with manufacturing systems to classify incidents, retrieve relevant knowledge from SOPs and maintenance records, and take appropriate actions such as guiding operators or escalating issues to maintenance teams.
Organisation
Dassault Systèmes is a French global software company specializing in 3D design, simulation, product lifecycle management (PLM), and virtual twin solutions for industries such as aerospace, automotive, and manufacturing. The company’s 3DEXPERIENCE platform provides a unified environment for modelling, engineering, and operations. A key focus of Dassault Systèmes is on “Virtual Twins” – scientific, data-driven digital models of real-world products and production systems. These virtual twins integrate real-time data to simulate behaviour, enabling enhanced process control and continuous optimization across the product lifecycle. Dassault Systèmes has publicly described virtual twins as the “cornerstone of the next industrial revolution,” combining modelling, simulation, and AI to drive smarter manufacturing.
Within Dassault Systèmes, the NETVIBES team (part of the Information Intelligence brand) delivers data analytics and AI-driven insights. NETVIBES provides a data science platform that “transforms massive information flows into actionable insights” and “augments the virtual twin experience with contextualized real-world data”. In practice, NETVIBES products allow business and engineering users to visualize and analyse data from multiple sources (IoT, ERP,
maintenance logs, etc.) in dashboards and AI models. For example, Dassault Aviation (the aircraft manufacturer) uses 3DEXPERIENCE NETVIBES to maximize fleet availability by feeding operational data through NETVIBES’s data science portfolio. Another NETVIBES solution called “AI-Maximized Asset Performance” applies machine learning and feedback loops to optimize asset uptime across a fleet. In short, NETVIBES combines big data, AI/ML, and Dassault’s virtual twin concepts to deliver manufacturing insights and automated decision support. (Notably, Dassault Systèmes merged its EXALEAD data search technology into the NETVIBES brand in 2021.)
Area of Computer Science
This project lies at the intersection of multiple domains within Computer Science, including:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) – for intelligent decision-making and automation
Natural Language Processing (NLP) – for understanding operator-reported issues and system logs

To automatically classify machine incidents as mechanical, electrical, or safety-related, enabling appropriate prioritization and efficient handling of reported issues.

1 Introduction

must be tightened to an exact torque specification. Deviations whether under-torque or
over-torque constitute quality incidents that require immediate assessment and correc-

With advancements in Artificial Intelligence, Large Language Models (LLMs), and
intelligent automation, it is now possible to design systems that assist or entirely replace
manual triage for routine torque incidents. This project, developed during my current
internship at Dassault Syst`emes Global Services Pvt. Ltd., Pune, focuses on building
Torque Assistant: an intelligent, agent-based incident resolution system for torque
quality monitoring in manufacturing. The system leverages LLMs, Retrieval-Augmented
Generation (RAG), and a multi-agent workflow orchestrated via LangGraph to auto-
matically validate torque events, classify severity, retrieve relevant Standard Operating
Procedures (SOPs) and historical incident records, and take appropriate resolution ac-
tions without requiring human intervention for routine cases.
Dassault Syst`emes is a French multinational software company specialising in 3D
design, simulation, and Product Lifecycle Management (PLM). Its flagship 3DEXPERI-
ENCE platform serves industries including aerospace, automotive, and industrial equip-
ment. A core concept is the Virtual Twin — a data-driven digital replica of a real-world
product or production system that integrates live sensor data to simulate behaviour and
enable predictive control. The NETVIBES division (part of the Information Intelligence
brand) provides data analytics and AI-driven insights on top of this infrastructure. This
project is situated within the NETVIBES initiative to embed intelligent automation into

2 Literature Survey
ResearchinintelligentmanufacturinghasincreasinglymovedtowardAI-assisteddecision-
making for anomaly detection and incident resolution. Early work on rule-based expert
systems for fault diagnosis [1] established the principle of encoding domain knowledge for
automatedtriage,butsuchsystemswerebrittleanddifficulttomaintainasmanufacturing
environments evolved.
The emergence of neural information retrieval gave rise to Retrieval-Augmented Gen-
eration (RAG), introduced by Lewis et al. [2], which grounds generative model outputs
in a retrieved evidence set. This is particularly well-suited to industrial domains where
decisions must be traceable to authoritative documents such as SOPs and maintenance
manuals, rather than relying on model parametric memory alone.
Advances in LLM-based agent architectures [3, 4] have demonstrated that language
models can serve not only as generators but as reasoning engines capable of tool use,
multi-step planning, and conditional branching. The LangGraph framework [5] extends
1

this to stateful, graph-based multi-agent pipelines, enabling workflows where specialised
agents hand off context through a shared typed state directly applicable to sequential
incident triage.
For scalable similarity search over high-dimensional embeddings, Johnson et al. [6]
introducedFAISS(FacebookAISimilaritySearch), enablingsub-linearnearest-neighbour
retrieval over large corpora. This underpins the dual vector store architecture used in
Torque Assistant for SOP and past-incident retrieval.
In the domain of manufacturing AI, Dassault Syst`emes has positioned the Virtual
Twin as the foundation for next-generation industrial intelligence [7], with NETVIBES
providing the AI layer connecting real-time sensor streams, predictive models, and oper-
ational dashboards. The present project builds upon these foundations at the incident-
resolution layer, targeting the specific bottleneck of manual torque quality triage [8].
3 Problem Definition
Manufacturing assembly lines generate large volumes of torque fastening events per pro-
duction shift. Each event records whether a bolted joint was tightened within the torque
andangletolerancesspecifiedinengineeringSOPs. Whenaneventfallsoutsidetolerance,
it is flagged as a quality incident requiring investigation and resolution.
The current manual approach suffers from several structural limitations. Engineers
must retrieve the relevant SOP for each affected joint, assess deviation severity based on
experience, consult historical incidents for precedent, and decide on a resolution action.
This process introduces queue delays, produces inconsistent severity assessments across
engineers, and fails to differentiate between minor deviations on non-critical joints and
genuine safety failures. Furthermore, relevant SOP clauses and historical incident reso-
lutions are stored across disparate documents and logs, making knowledge retrieval slow
and unreliable.
The core problem addressed by this project is: Can a multi-agent AI system reliably
automate the full torque incident triage pipeline from raw event validation through sever-
ity classification, SOP-grounded reasoning, and resolution action while enforcing a safe,
auditable decision policy that correctly handles safety-critical joints?
The system must handle variability in joint types, tolerate imperfect data (unknown
joints, missing SOP entries), scale to batch processing of hundreds of events per run, and
provide a traceable decision audit trail for quality engineers.

2. To build a multi-agent LangGraph workflow that routes each incident through a
structured pipeline of specialised nodes: Validator → Severity Classifier → Auto-
Close Router → RAG Retrieval Agent → Decision Logic Agent → Action Agent.

5 Methodology
The system follows a modular, graph-based architecture where each processing stage is
encapsulated as an independent node within a LangGraph state machine. The shared
state object, IncidentState, is a typed Pydantic model that carries the torque event
data, computed validation fields, retrieved RAG context, and the final agent result across
all nodes.
Data Pipeline
TorqueeventrecordsarestoredasCSV(data/torque events.csv), withfieldsincluding
event id,jointname,targetandactualtorqueinNm,tolerance,andanglereadings. SOP
specifications are stored in data/sops.json, encoding per-joint engineering tolerances
and the safety critical flag. A separate data/sop chunks.json stores paragraph-
levelSOPtextfordensevectorretrieval,anddata/past incidents.jsonholdshistorical
resolution examples. All datasets are generated synthetically by generate data.py with
controllable anomaly rates.
Vector Store Construction
Atstartup, twoFAISSvectorstoresarebuiltusingOpenAIembeddingsviacore/rag.py:
oneoverSOPprocedurechunks(build vector store)andoneoverpastincidentrecords
(build incident vector store). A joint-to-safety-critical lookup dictionary is also pre-
computed from sops.json to avoid per-event file I/O during batch runs.
3

Workflow Nodes
1. Validator: Computes whether the actual torque and angle fall within the SOP-
defined tolerance band. Sets the validation field (PASS/FAIL) and populates a
structured deviation summary.
2. Severity Classifier: For failed events, invokes an LLM with the deviation data
and safety-critical flag to assign a severity level: LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, or CRITICAL.
3. Auto-Close Router: If severity is LOW and the joint is not safety-critical, the
event is auto-closed without further LLM calls preserving API quota for genuinely
complex cases.
4. RAG Retrieval Agent: Retrieves the top-k most relevant SOP chunks and past
incident summaries using cosine similarity search over the dual FAISS indices.
5. Decision Logic Agent: An LLM-backed agent that receives the full incident con-
textdeviationmetrics, severity, retrievedSOPclauses, andanalogouspastincidents
and produces a structured resolution recommendation: operator guidance, CMMS
ticket creation, or escalation.
6. Action Agent: Executes the recommended actions, logs them to RUN LOG via
core/tools.py, and writes the final agent result into the shared state.
Batch Runner and Reporting
main.py provides a CLI batch runner that processes configurable event volumes, prints
a compact per-event status line including the node path taken, and saves a structured
JSON report via core/reporter.py. A --verbose flag enables DEBUG-level logging to
expose LLM reasoning chains, RAG retrieval results, and tool calls.
Streamlit Dashboard
app.py exposes the system as an interactive Streamlit web application with a per-event
node-by-node decision inspector and batch-level Plotly analytics covering severity distri-
bution, auto-close rate, and workflow path breakdown.

% This IEEEtran.bst features a very powerful and flexible mechanism for
% controlling the capitalization, punctuation, spacing, quotation, and
% newlines of the formatted entry fields. (Note: IEEEtran.bst does not need
% or use the newline/newblock feature, but it has been implemented for
% possible future use.) The output states of IEEEtran.bst consist of
% multiple independent attributes and, as such, can be thought of as being
% vectors, rather than the simple scalar values ("before.all", 
% "mid.sentence", etc.) used in most other .bst files.
% 
% The more flexible and complex design used here was motivated in part by
% IEEE's rather unusual bibliography style. For example, IEEE ends the
% previous field item with a period and large space prior to the publisher
% address; the @electronic entry types use periods as inter-item punctuation
% rather than the commas used by the other entry types; and URLs are never
% followed by periods even though they are the last item in the entry.
% Although it is possible to accommodate these features with the conventional
% output state system, the seemingly endless exceptions make for convoluted,
% unreliable and difficult to maintain code.
%
% IEEEtran.bst's output state system can be easily understood via a simple
% illustration of two most recently formatted entry fields (on the stack):
%
%               CURRENT_ITEM
%               "PREVIOUS_ITEM
%
% which, in this example, is to eventually appear in the bibliography as:
% 
%               "PREVIOUS_ITEM," CURRENT_ITEM
%
% It is the job of the output routine to take the previous item off of the
% stack (while leaving the current item at the top of the stack), apply its
% trailing punctuation (including closing quote marks) and spacing, and then
% to write the result to BibTeX's output buffer:
% 
%               "PREVIOUS_ITEM," 
% 
% Punctuation (and spacing) between items is often determined by both of the
% items rather than just the first one. The presence of quotation marks
% further complicates the situation because, in standard English, trailing
% punctuation marks are supposed to be contained within the quotes.
% 
% IEEEtran.bst maintains two output state (aka "status") vectors which
% correspond to the previous and current (aka "this") items. Each vector
% consists of several independent attributes which track punctuation,
% spacing, quotation, and newlines. Capitalization status is handled by a
% separate scalar because the format routines, not the output routine,
% handle capitalization and, therefore, there is no need to maintain the
% capitalization attribute for both the "previous" and "this" items.
% 
% When a format routine adds a new item, it copies the current output status
% vector to the previous output status vector and (usually) resets the
% current (this) output status vector to a "standard status" vector. Using a
% "standard status" vector in this way allows us to redefine what we mean by
% "standard status" at the start of each entry handler and reuse the same
% format routines under the various inter-item separation schemes. For
% example, the standard status vector for the @book entry type may use
% commas for item separators, while the @electronic type may use periods,
% yet both entry handlers exploit many of the exact same format routines.
% 
% Because format routines have write access to the output status vector of
% the previous item, they can override the punctuation choices of the
% previous format routine! Therefore, it becomes trivial to implement rules
% such as "Always use a period and a large space before the publisher." By
% pushing the generation of the closing quote mark to the output routine, we
% avoid all the problems caused by having to close a quote before having all
% the information required to determine what the punctuation should be.
%
% The IEEEtran.bst output state system can easily be expanded if needed.
% For instance, it is easy to add a "space.tie" attribute value if the
% bibliography rules mandate that two items have to be joined with an
% unbreakable space.

ote$ * edition * quote$ *
              " may be too high (or improper) for conversion" * " in " * cite$ * warning$
            }
          if$
        }
      if$
    }
  if$
}

% Here we write out all the LaTeX code that we will need. The most involved
% code sequences are those that control the alternate interword spacing and
% foreign language hyphenation patterns. The heavy use of \providecommand
% gives users a way to override the defaults. Special thanks to Javier Bezos,
% Johannes Braams, Robin Fairbairns, Heiko Oberdiek, Donald Arseneau and all
% the other gurus on comp.text.tex for their help and advice on the topic of
% \selectlanguage, Babel and BibTeX.
FUNCTION {begin.bib}
{ "% Generated by IEEEtran.bst, version: " bst.file.version * " (" * bst.file.date * ")" *
  write$ newline$
  preamble$ empty$ 'skip$
    { preamble$ write$ newline$ }
  if$
  "\begin{thebibliography}{"  longest.label  * "}" *
  write$ newline$
  "\providecommand{\url}[1]{#1}"
  write$ newline$
  "\csname url@samestyle\endcsname"
  write$ newline$
  "\providecommand{\newblock}{\relax}"
  write$ newline$
  "\providecommand{\bibinfo}[2]{#2}"
  write$ newline$
  "\providecommand{\BIBentrySTDinterwordspacing}{\spaceskip=0pt\relax}"
  write$ newline$
  "\providecommand{\BIBentryALTinterwordstretchfactor}{"
  ALTinterwordstretchfactor * "}" *
  write$ newline$
  "\providecommand{\BIBentryALTinterwordspacing}{\spaceskip=\fontdimen2\font plus "
  write$ newline$
  "\BIBentryALTinterwordstretchfactor\fontdimen3\font minus \fontdimen4\font\relax}"
  write$ newline$
  "\providecommand{\BIBforeignlanguage}[2]{{%"
  write$ newline$
  "\expandafter\ifx\csname l@#1\endcsname\relax"
  write$ newline$
  "\typeout{** WARNING: IEEEtran.bst: No hyphenation pattern has been}%"
  write$ newline$
  "\typeout{** loaded for the language `#1'. Using the pattern for}%"
  write$ newline$
  "\typeout{** the default language instead.}%"
  write$ newline$
  "\else"
  write$ newline$
  "\language=\csname l@#1\endcsname"
  write$ newline$
  "\fi"
  write$ newline$
  "#2}}"
  write$ newline$
  "\providecommand{\BIBdecl}{\relax}"
  write$ newline$
  "\BIBdecl"
  write$ newline$
}

%% edition/title

% Note: IEEE considers the edition to be closely associated with
% the title of a book. So, in IEEEtran.bst the edition is normally handled 
% within the formatting of the title. The format.edition function is 
% retained here for possible future use.
FUNCTION {format.edition}
{ edition duplicate$ empty$ 'skip$
    { this.to.prev.status
      this.status.std
      convert.edition
      status.cap
        { "t" }
        { "l" }
      if$ change.case$
      "edition" bibinfo.check
      "~" * bbl.edition *
      cap.status.std
    }
  if$
}

% This is used to format the booktitle of a conference proceedings.
% Here we use the "intype" field to provide the user a way to 
% override the word "in" (e.g., with things like "presented at")
% Use of intype stops the emphasis of the booktitle to indicate that
% we no longer mean the written conference proceedings, but the
% conference itself.
FUNCTION {format.in.booktitle}
{ booktitle "booktitle" bibinfo.check duplicate$ empty$ 'skip$
    { this.to.prev.status
      this.status.std
      select.language
      intype missing$
        { emphasize
          bbl.in " " *
        }
        { intype " " * }
      if$
      swap$ *
      cap.status.std
    }
  if$
}

% This is used to format the booktitle of collection.
% Here the "intype" field is not supported, but "edition" is.
FUNCTION {format.in.booktitle.edition}
{ booktitle "booktitle" bibinfo.check duplicate$ empty$ 'skip$
    { this.to.prev.status
      this.status.std
      select.language
      emphasize
      edition empty$ 'skip$
        { ", " *
          edition
          convert.edition
          "l" change.case$
          * "~" * bbl.edition *
        }
      if$
      bbl.in " " * swap$ *
      cap.status.std
    }
  if$
}

Practice school / Project work – guidelines (2025_26 Batch)
(CSE 4299 / ICT4292 / DSE4292 )
As a part of the 8th Semester practice school/project work, students must carry out project work
for a minimum period of 4 months, or up to 6 or 12 months. Students may carry out external
projects at Industry/Academia or internal projects in MIT, Manipal. The project should extend
current knowledge in the chosen area by providing an implementation/ tool/application using
the research results/existing technologies.
General instruction
• The start date for Practice school / Project work is 03.01.2026. All internal project
students should report to the Department on 03.01.2026.
• Those students who require the bonafide certificate for applying for internships can get
it from the Associate Dean – B office with a formal request letter.
• All students once notified with the Internal guide list are expected to communicate
with their guide and inform them if they have an external company offer or will join
college as Internal project student etc.
• Both internal and external students are advised not to change their internal guides unless
otherwise approved by Associate Dean for genuine reasons.
• B.Tech honors students will report to both the project mentor and faculty mentor
assigned earlier. The project mentors will take care of all evaluation procedures, while
the earlier mentor will be associated with them regarding BTech honors completion
procedures, including publication.
• Both internal and external students are expected to submit the Project Synopsis Report
as per the format provided by 20.01.2026. Students are expected to communicate the
softcopy of their synopsis to their internal guide four days before the deadline for
verification and acknowledgment by their internal guide.
• Project diary and other project-related documents are to be submitted to your Project
Guide as per the format provided from time to time.
• The final project report should be prepared in consultation with the guide. Students
must avoid plagiarism(AI and Regular) with an allowed limit of 20% using Turnitin.
Throughout the report, others' work should be acknowledged by proper citation.
Students are expected to communicate the softcopy of their final report to their internal
guide.
• The naming convention for all project-related documents shall be like
regno_studentname_documentname.pdf. Ex. 200905026_ashok_synopis.pdf.
• Midterm and final evaluation break-up marks with various parameters are attached for
students’ reference and preparedness. Any clarification regarding project work shall be
done with respective internal guides only.
• Synopsis, mid-term and Final Reports shall be in soft copy.
General instruction for internal project students
• Students must go through Scopus/Web-of-science indexed journal publications in
computer science and engineering and identify a topic in consultation with the internal
guide.

Web link to access the papers:
OpenAthens (SSO - Single Sign-on) - Remote Access to e-Resources
https://go.openathens.net/redirector/manipal.edu?url=https%3A%2F%2Flib
portal.manipal.edu%2FMIT%2FMIT.aspx
(Step by-step procedure is given as a separate annexure)
• The project work can be carried out individually or in a group of two. However, each
group member must submit a separate synopsis/project report. Evaluation will be based
on individual team member’s contributions, so team members must contribute equally
while involved in the group project.
• The schedule and lab in which the internal project should be done will be communicated
tentatively by the 4th week of December 2025.
• Internal project students are advised to discuss with their internal guide and confirm the
domain with which they are likely to do their project with their internal guide by
08.01.2026.
• Internal students can avail themselves of an exciting opportunity to be part of the
different funded projects ongoing in the department toward innovation, research, and
development. This initiative will provide you with a platform to enhance your skills,
gain hands-on experience, and contribute to impactful work. Interested internal students
can communicate with their internal guides and get more details to carry further if there
is opening for these funded projects. The respective internal guides will connect you
with the principal investigators of the funded project. Some of the funded projects are
given below for reference.
1. Indian Language to Indian Language Machine Translation (Dr Narendra VG )
2. Discourse Integrated Dravidian Language to Dravidian Language Machine Translation (Prof Ashwath
Rao B )
3. Development and validation of a Deep Learning Model to diagnose Coronary Artery Disease from CT
Coronary Angiography Images (Manjunath K N)
4. Centre of Indian Language Data (COIL-D) (Dr Murali Krishna)
5. AI based Document Retrieval (Dr. Manohara Pai M M)
6. AI based Healthcare Innovation (Dr. Manohara Pai M M)
7. AI based Cybersecurity- Threat model Generation, Vulnerability detection and prediction, ethical hacking
in ICS (Dr. Manohara Pai M M)
There are some more funded projects available with our School faculty. Please contact respective
internal guides for more information and connect to those Principal Investigators.
• Also, we have a product development team focusing on new product development
activities within the School and internal students can be part of it and carry out their
practice school projects. Students should again contact their respective internal guide
and get more details.
• The internal project students shall do projects in marketing, HR, management, etc.,
provided the concerned student has a co-guide from the respective department (e.g., co-
guide from the Humanities department in case the project is related to management).
Students should also inform the other department co-guide that they must attend all the
presentations along with the School faculty stream. To approve such projects, students
should produce an authorization letter from the other department co-guide and HOD to
the School internal guide.

• The internal project students are expected to maintain an exclusive project observation
notebook, update their work daily, and take signatures from project lab faculty. In
addition, they are expected to show their project observation notebook to their internal
guide every week, discuss their project progress, and take signatures. The internal guide
will note your weekly update of project progress and reflect in project rubrics marking
during midterm and final project evaluation.
• In addition, the internal project students must update their project progress in the project
diary once every 15 days. Also, students should give their project update presentation
to their internal guide.
• Your internal guide will inform you of the timing and venue for the midterm, and final
presentations. The time limit for the midterm and final viva will be 20 minutes,
followed by a Q&A session. The designated faculty stream will take the mid-term and
final viva.
• The students are expected to complete the project work, satisfy all the objectives, and
meet the required criteria by the last instructional day of the semester.
Semester Abroad Program: Student Instructions
• Students must begin their Research Internship at MIT from 2nd January 2026.
• The internship work must be carried out in OFFLINE mode before departure.
• Students must complete the mid-term viva before leaving for their semester abroad.
• During their semester abroad, students shall continue the research internship in
ONLINE mode.
• Evaluation will be conducted by MIT, and students will be graded based on their
research progress.
• The final internship viva will be scheduled in July 2026.
General instruction for external / Industry project students
• In the synopsis, students must keep a copy of their project internship offer letter
provided by the company mentioning both start and end dates.
• Students must update the internal guide about the progress made using a project diary
once every 15 days, which will be a part of the evaluation.
• The students who have signed an NDA (Non-disclosure agreement with the company)
must follow the SOP on Practice School defined by the institute. An additional project
must be completed in consultation with their internal guide apart from the project work
done at the company. Students are advised to take up industry projects offering offline
internships. However, online internships are also allowed, provided relevant
information is discussed and confirmed with their internal guides.
• The students are expected to complete the project work satisfying all the project
objectives before the last instructional day of the semester, with the exception given to
those carrying out 5 or 6-month projects.
• Any student who is undergoing project work in the industry with feedback that,
he/she is not performing well / not regular to the company etc. as reported by the
external Industry supervisor will be notified to drop the internship and to continue
their project work (as internal project) in the department.

• Students who are allowed to do their projects abroad and in industry shall give their
midterm presentation through MS Teams. However, they must give their final
presentation in person only. All others should give both midterm / final presentations
in person. The time limit for midterm and final viva will be 20 minutes, followed by
viva.
• Students pursuing their project work abroad, shall give their final viva through online
mode with due permission from their internal guide and project coordinator(s).
Instructions for NDA-Signed Students
It is advised that, students undergoing external company projects who signed NDA
should complete an additional project in the Department under their internal guide
mentorship and the report of the work should be kept in their project report as additional
chapter with title, “Additional Project” with following sections:
1. Abstract
2. Introduction
3. Methodology
4. Results and discussion
5. Conclusion
6. References
This chapter should be placed after the reference section of the company project. Please
be informed that the company details of the project should contain details of where you
are interning and not with details of MIT.

IMPLEMENTATION PLAN: PROJECT REGENAI (RAPTOR-BASED)
Objective: To transform a disorganized, "messy" local directory or wiki into a
structured, semantically categorized, and fully summarized corporate repository
using a local-first AI pipeline.
1. Core Tech Stack (100% Local & Open-Source)
Layer Component Technical Selection
Intelligence Local LLM Engine Ollama running Llama 3.1 (8B or 70B)
Parsing Document Unstructured.io (Local Library)
Extraction
Math Embedding Model BAAI/bge-m3 (State-of-the-art for local
retrieval)
Clustering Recursive Logic Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM) via Scikit-
Learn
Storage Vector Database ChromaDB (Persistent local storage)
2. Detailed Phase-by-Phase Pipeline
Phase 1: Advanced Data Ingestion
 The Action: The system takes a local Path as input and recursively walks the
directory.
 Implementation: We use Unstructured.io to "clean" raw files (.pptx, .py, .xlsx,
.pdf).
 Technique: Instead of simple splitting, we use Semantic Chunking. The system
looks for "thematic breaks" in text so that a single chunk doesn't lose its
meaning, ensuring high-quality embeddings.

Phase 2: Recursive Semantic Clustering (The RAPTOR Loop)
 The Action: Building the "Tree" from the bottom up.
 Implementation: 1. Level 0: Embed all file chunks.
2. Clustering: Use GMM to group these chunks. GMM allows "Soft Clustering,"
meaning a file can belong to a primary folder while acknowledging it relates to
another.
3. Summarization: Feed each cluster of text to the Local LLM. The LLM writes a 1-
paragraph summary of what these files are about.
4. Recursion: Embed those summaries and cluster them again to create "Parent
Folders."
Phase 3: Validation & The "Confidence Loop"
 The Action: Ensuring the math meets the 70-90% threshold.
 Implementation: We calculate the BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion) or
Silhouette Score.
 The Retry: If the score is $<0.7$, the script automatically adjusts the number of
clusters and re-runs Phase 2 until the groups are mathematically "tight" and
logical.
Phase 4: Summary Generation & Meta-Tagging
 The Action: Final polish of the content.
 Implementation: For every file moved to the new structure, the LLM generates a
concise "Executive Summary" and a list of key topics. This summary is what the
"Higher-o(cid:431)s" will see to understand the file without opening it.

4. Final Output Deliverables
1. Regenerated Directory: A brand new, clean physical folder structure created on
the local drive.
2. Manifest File (README.md / Structure.json): A file in every folder containing the
LLM-generated summary of that folder's purpose and the files within it.
3. Audit Log: A report showing the "Before vs. After" and the confidence scores for
the clustering.

The 4-Step RAPTOR Loop
Step 1: Leaf Node Creation (The Foundation)
We take your messy local files and break them into small "leaf nodes" (chunks).
 Local Action: Use Unstructured.io to extract text from your .pptx, .py, etc.
 Vectorizing: We convert these chunks into numbers (embeddings) using your local
BGE-M3 model.
At this stage, we have thousands of tiny data points representing every sentence/paragraph
in your messy wiki.
Step 2: GMM Clustering (Finding the Siblings)
RAPTOR uses Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM) for clustering.
 The Logic: Unlike K-Means, GMM allows for "soft clustering." A file about "Python
Finance Scripts" might belong 80% to the "Code" cluster and 20% to the "Finance"
cluster.
 The Threshold: This is where we calculate your 70–90% confidence score. If the
files in a cluster aren't "dense" enough, we retry.
Step 3: Abstractive Summarization (Naming the Folder)
This is the "Magic" step where your Local LLM (Llama 3) comes in.
 The Action: We feed all the text chunks from one cluster into the LLM.
 The Prompt: "Read these 10 files and write a 100-word executive summary that
captures the main project goals."
 Result: This summary becomes a new data point (a "Parent Node") that represents
all those files combined.
Step 4: The Recursion (Building the Tree)
This is the "Recursive" part of RAPTOR.
 The Loop: We take the summaries we just created in Step 3 and treat them like
new files.
 Repeat: We embed those summaries, cluster them again, and summarize the
clusters of summaries.

 Stop Condition: We keep doing this until we have one single "Root" summary that
describes the entire Wiki.
How it Regenerates Your Structure
Once the RAPTOR tree is built, we "flip" it to create your new local folder structure:
1. Level 1 (Top Level): The summaries from the highest level of the tree become your
Main Category Folders (e.g., /Corporate_Strategy/).
2. Level 2 (Mid Level): The summaries from the middle layers become your Sub-
folders (e.g., /Corporate_Strategy/Financial_Audit_2025/).
3. Level 3 (Bottom Level): The original files are moved into these folders based on
which "Leaf Node" cluster they belonged to.

# Inventory: Crawl and Extract Content  
First, recursively traverse the input directory (e.g. with Python’s `os.walk`) to list all files and subfolders.  Identify relevant file types (source code files like `.py`, `.js`, `.java`, `.cpp`, documentation files like `.md`, `.txt`, `.pdf`, etc.). For each file type, use a suitable parser to extract text (and optionally metadata).  For example, **Apache Tika** can extract text from most document formats (PDF, DOCX, PPT, etc.) and even returns metadata (creation date, author, format, language)【34†L47-L55】【34†L53-L57】.  Plain text or code files can be read directly (or tokenized via a library like Tree-sitter for code).  Store each file’s content (and metadata tags) for processing.  *Key point:* capturing metadata (file names, paths, timestamps) can aid downstream grouping and citation.

# Chunking and Embedding  
Split each document into smaller, context-sized “chunks” before embedding.  A strong chunking strategy is crucial: too large and you exceed model limits, too small and you lose context.  Common methods include **fixed-size splits with overlap** (e.g. every 500–1000 tokens with 100–200 token overlap) and **semantic splits** at logical boundaries (paragraphs, sentence breaks, or code function/class boundaries)【5†L281-L290】【5†L388-L391】.  Semantic splitting often yields more coherent chunks.  As Databricks notes, chunking “segments complex data into more digestible pieces,” which “improves retrieval accuracy” in a RAG pipeline【5†L244-L252】.  After splitting, convert each chunk into an embedding using a model (e.g. OpenAI’s text-embedding-ada or a Sentence Transformer).  Store all embeddings in a vector database (e.g. Pinecone, FAISS, Weaviate). In a typical RAG/embedding workflow, one **indexes** each chunk by embedding and storing it in the vector store, then later **retrieves** relevant chunks via similarity search【5†L269-L272】.

Store all embeddings in a vector database (e.g. Pinecone, FAISS, Weaviate). In a typical RAG/embedding workflow, one **indexes** each chunk by embedding and storing it in the vector store, then later **retrieves** relevant chunks via similarity search【5†L269-L272】.

# Clustering and Scoring  
With all chunks embedded, group semantically similar chunks together. You can apply any clustering algorithm on the embedding vectors – for example, **K-Means** or **DBSCAN** on cosine distances.  Another approach is Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs), which “softly assign” each chunk to clusters and yield a probability (confidence) for membership【38†L193-L198】.  In practice, choose an algorithm and number of clusters (or use hierarchical/DBSCAN to determine clusters).  For each cluster, compute a quality or confidence score.  One option is the **silhouette coefficient**, which measures how well a point fits its cluster vs. the nearest other cluster (range −1 to 1)【11†L258-L266】. A high silhouette means the cluster is cohesive and well-separated. Alternatively, if using GMM, use the membership probability as a confidence.  The goal is to ensure each cluster truly represents one “topic” or subproject. Clusters will group files and code chunks about the same topic; for instance, one cluster might contain all chunks related to “database access”, another “UI components”, etc. Embedding models facilitate this: as Noel Benji writes, “Sentence Transformers transform text into vectors, preserving semantic relationships” so that similar items (e.g. documents about similar themes) end up nearby in vector space【8†L157-L164】.  (Similarly, embedding research shows raw data become “dense vector representations” that unlock clustering【8†L55-L60】.)

# Generating Summaries with an LLM  
For each cluster of related chunks, generate a summary of that topic.  You can use a retrieval-augmented approach: retrieve the most representative chunks of the cluster and feed them to an LLM with an instructive prompt. The prompt could say: *“Given the following code and documentation snippets all about *\<topic\>*, write a concise summary of what this part of the project does, mentioning key functions/files.”* Depending on needs, you might do this hierarchically: first generate a **chunk-level** summary for each chunk, then aggregate those into a **cluster-level** summary (a “map-reduce” or hierarchical summarization approach【42†L293-L299】).  In fact, recent research on code repositories uses exactly this two-phase strategy: break code into 5k-token chunks, summarize each, then summarize those summaries into a higher-level overview【42†L293-L299】.  Another method is directly prompting the LLM on all chunk texts (if under context limit) or on their key sentences. A blended extractive/abstractive strategy often works best【39†L38-L47】: use LLM to highlight key points (abstractive) but ensure grounding by including actual excerpts from the chunks (extractive elements).

A blended extractive/abstractive strategy often works best【39†L38-L47】: use LLM to highlight key points (abstractive) but ensure grounding by including actual excerpts from the chunks (extractive elements).

If multiple clusters correspond to different subprojects or topics, you may optionally feed the project’s directory structure (file tree) or cluster labels as additional context to the LLM to help organize the summary. In any case, instruct the LLM to cite or reference the source when needed.  (One could even include file paths or headings from the chunks as “citations” in the generated markdown.) Ensure the prompt requests a structured markdown output with links or references to the original chunks.

# Validation and Refinement  
Finally, **validate** the generated summaries against the source files. LLMs can hallucinate or omit details【19†L129-L137】, so cross-check facts. For example, verify that every claim in the summary appears in some chunk. Metrics like ROUGE or overlap scores (comparing summary to chunk content) can give a rough automatic check of coverage【30†L105-L114】. More importantly, manually review or have a human (or another model) confirm factual consistency – as Microsoft notes, evaluation should consider *fluency, coherence, relevance,* and especially *factual consistency*【30†L49-L53】. Adjust the pipeline as needed: if a cluster is too broad, split it; if summary missed key code, refine the prompt or include more chunk text. Testing with different prompts (zero-shot vs. few-shot) is also advised: one study finds “testing under different prompting strategies may be important to see which prompts give the best results”【20†L1-L4】. Iterate until the summaries accurately reflect the source.

**Summary:** In practice, you will (1) crawl the directory and extract all text (using tools like Tika for documents)【34†L47-L55】; (2) intelligently split each file into chunks (favoring semantic boundaries) and embed them【5†L244-L252】【5†L388-L391】; (3) cluster these embeddings (e.g. via K-means or GMM) and score each cluster for cohesion (silhouette, GMM probability)【11†L258-L266】【38†L193-L198】; (4) for each cluster, feed the chunk texts to an LLM (using RAG or map-reduce summarization) to generate a detailed markdown summary, citing sources; and (5) validate the output (fact-check against files, adjust clusters or prompts)【19†L129-L137】【30†L49-L53】. # digit-rss-tracker - Setup Guide

Repository to track an author on digit and notify when he posts an article (made to track a goated friend named vyom ramani)

## What you're setting up

A Python script that runs daily on your Hetzner server, checks Vyom's RSS feed
on digit.in, and sends a push notification to your phone via ntfy when a new
article is posted.

The script validates the feed is reachable before doing anything, stores a list
of articles it's already notified you about, and only pings you for new ones.

---

## Before you start — what you need on your machine

You already ran test_feed.py locally and confirmed the feed works. Good.
Now you just need to SSH into your server. On Mac, Terminal is all you need —
it's built in, no extra software required.

---

## Step 1 — Phone setup (do this first)

1. Install the **ntfy** app on your phone:
   - Android: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=io.heckel.ntfy
   - iOS: https://apps.apple.com/app/ntfy/id1625396347

2. Open the app → tap the "+" button → enter a topic name
   - A topic is just your personal notification channel — like a secret radio
     frequency. Anyone who knows the name can subscribe, so make it hard to guess.
   - Good example: vyom-digit-ansh-7k3x2
   - Bad example: vyom or digit (too guessable)
   - Write it down — you'll need it in Step 4

---

## Step 2 — SSH into your server

Open Terminal on your Mac and run:

ssh root@YOUR_SERVER_IP

Replace YOUR_SERVER_IP with your Hetzner server's IP address.
You'll be dropped into a command prompt on your server.

---

## Step 3 — Create the project folder and add the script

Create a folder for the project:

mkdir -p ~/digit-rss-tracker
    cd ~/digit-rss-tracker

Now open a new file called checker.py in nano (a simple terminal text editor):

nano checker.py

Paste the full contents of checker.py here, then:

- Ctrl+O → Enter (saves the file)
- Ctrl+X (exits nano)

---

## Step 4 — Set your ntfy topic in the script

Open the script again:

nano checker.py

Find this line near the top:

NTFY_TOPIC = "YOUR_SECRET_TOPIC_HERE"

Change it to your actual topic name from Step 1, e.g.:

NTFY_TOPIC = "vyom-digit-ansh-7k3x2"

Save and exit (Ctrl+O → Enter → Ctrl+X).

---

## Step 5 — Install dependencies

Your server needs two Python libraries. Run these commands:

# Check Python 3 is available — should print something like 3.10.x or 3.11.x
    python3 --version

# Install pip (Python's package manager) if it's not already there
    sudo apt update && sudo apt install python3-pip -y

# Install the two libraries the script uses:
    # feedparser → reads and parses RSS feeds
    # requests   → makes HTTP calls (used for both feed fetching and ntfy notification)
    pip3 install feedparser requests --break-system-packages

The --break-system-packages flag is needed on newer Ubuntu versions — it just
tells pip it's okay to install into the system Python environment.

---

## Step 6 — Run the script manually to test it

cd ~/digit-rss-tracker
    python3 checker.py

Expected output on first run:

HTTP calls (used for both feed fetching and ntfy notification)
    pip3 install feedparser requests --break-system-packages

The --break-system-packages flag is needed on newer Ubuntu versions — it just
tells pip it's okay to install into the system Python environment.

---

## Step 6 — Run the script manually to test it

cd ~/digit-rss-tracker
    python3 checker.py

Expected output on first run:

─── Digit Article Checker ───
    [→] Validating feed: https://www.digit.in/author/vyomramani/feed/
    [✓] Feed is valid. Found 10 articles in feed.
    [✓] Notified: Sam Altman investigation: 6 crazy revelations
    [✓] Notified: Sam Altman to blame? Why Microsoft and OpenAI are drifting apart
    ... (one line per article)
    [✓] Done — 10 new article(s) notified.
    ─────────────────────────────

Your phone will buzz for all 10 current articles — that's completely expected.
The script is marking them all as "already seen" so on every future run it only
notifies you about genuinely new ones.

If the feed is unreachable for any reason you'll see:

[✗] Feed validation failed: Feed URL returned HTTP 404.
        No notifications sent. Will try again next run.

---

## Step 7 — Set up the daily cron job

Cron is Linux's built-in task scheduler. You write one line telling it when to
run your script, and it handles it automatically forever — even after reboots.

Open the cron editor:

crontab -e

If it asks which editor to use, pick nano (option 1).

Add this line at the very bottom of the file:

0 9 * * * /usr/bin/python3 /root/digit-rss-tracker/checker.py >> /root/digit-rss-tracker/checker.log 2>&1

Breaking down what each part means:

0 9 * * *       → when to run. Format is: minute | hour | day | month | weekday
                      0 9 * * * = at minute 0 of hour 9 = 9:00 AM, every day
    /usr/bin/python3          → full path to Python. Cron needs full paths, not shortcuts
    /root/digit-rss-tracker/checker.py → your script, also full path
    >> checker.log            → append all printed output to a log file
    2>&1                      → also capture any errors into the same log file

Save and exit (Ctrl+O → Enter → Ctrl+X).
Cron will confirm: "crontab: installing new crontab"

---

## Changing the schedule

Want to check every 2 days instead of daily?

0 9 */2 * *     → 9am every 2 days

Every 12 hours:

0 */12 * * *    → midnight and noon every day

---

## Checking the log anytime

To see what the script has been doing:

cat ~/digit-rss-tracker/checker.log

Each run appends to this file so you have a full history.

---

## Files on your server after setup

~/digit-rss-tracker/
    ├── checker.py          ← the main script
    ├── seen_articles.txt   ← auto-created on first run, one URL per line
    └── checker.log         ← auto-created by cron, full run history

---

## Updating the author or ntfy topic

To track a different author, open checker.py and change FEED_URL at the top.
To change your ntfy topic, change NTFY_TOPIC and update your phone subscription.

        timeout=10,
        headers={"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; personal RSS reader)"},

    print(f"    HTTP Status : {response.status_code}")

import os
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from jose import JWTError, jwt
from passlib.context import CryptContext
from fastapi import HTTPException, Depends
from fastapi.security import HTTPBearer, HTTPAuthorizationCredentials

SECRET_KEY = os.getenv("SECRET_KEY", "changeme")
ALGORITHM = "HS256"
TOKEN_EXPIRE_DAYS = 30
APP_PASSWORD = os.getenv("APP_PASSWORD", "changeme")

pwd_context = CryptContext(schemes=["bcrypt"], deprecated="auto")
bearer = HTTPBearer()


def verify_password(plain: str) -> bool:
    return plain == APP_PASSWORD


def create_token() -> str:
    expire = datetime.utcnow() + timedelta(days=TOKEN_EXPIRE_DAYS)
    return jwt.encode({"exp": expire, "sub": "user"}, SECRET_KEY, algorithm=ALGORITHM)


def verify_token(credentials: HTTPAuthorizationCredentials = Depends(bearer)):
    try:
        jwt.decode(credentials.credentials, SECRET_KEY, algorithms=[ALGORITHM])
    except JWTError:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Invalid token")

import aiosqlite
import os

DB_PATH = os.getenv("DB_PATH", "./paisa.db")

CREATE_TABLES = """
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS wallets (
    id         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    name       TEXT NOT NULL,
    type       TEXT NOT NULL CHECK(type IN ('cash','debit','credit')),
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now'))
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS funding_events (
    id         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    wallet_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES wallets(id),
    amount     REAL NOT NULL,
    date       TEXT NOT NULL,
    note       TEXT,
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now'))
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS transactions (
    id             INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    wallet_id      INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES wallets(id),
    amount         REAL NOT NULL,
    description    TEXT NOT NULL,
    category       TEXT NOT NULL,
    payment_method TEXT NOT NULL,
    date           TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at     TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now'))
);
"""


async def get_db():
    async with aiosqlite.connect(DB_PATH) as db:
        db.row_factory = aiosqlite.Row
        yield db


async def init_db():
    async with aiosqlite.connect(DB_PATH) as db:
        await db.executescript(CREATE_TABLES)
        await db.commit()

        cursor = await db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM wallets")
        count = (await cursor.fetchone())[0]
        if count == 0:
            await db.execute(
                "INSERT INTO wallets (name, type) VALUES (?, ?), (?, ?)",
                ("Cash", "cash", "Debit", "debit"),
            )
            await db.commit()

from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends
from datetime import datetime
from app.database import get_db
from app.auth import verify_token

router = APIRouter(dependencies=[Depends(verify_token)])


@router.get("/api/dashboard")
async def get_dashboard(month: str = None, db=Depends(get_db)):
    if not month:
        month = datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m")

    start = f"{month}-01"
    year, mon = map(int, month.split("-"))
    if mon == 12:
        end = f"{year+1}-01-01"
    else:
        end = f"{year}-{mon+1:02d}-01"

    total_row = await (
        await db.execute(
            "SELECT COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0) as total FROM transactions WHERE date >= ? AND date < ?",
            (start, end),
        )
    ).fetchone()
    total_spent = total_row["total"]

    days_in_month = (
        datetime.strptime(end, "%Y-%m-%d") - datetime.strptime(start, "%Y-%m-%d")
    ).days
    daily_avg = total_spent / days_in_month if days_in_month > 0 else 0

    cat_cursor = await db.execute(
        "SELECT category, COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0) as total FROM transactions "
        "WHERE date >= ? AND date < ? GROUP BY category ORDER BY total DESC",
        (start, end),
    )
    by_category = [
        {"category": r["category"], "total": r["total"]}
        for r in await cat_cursor.fetchall()
    ]

    wallets_cursor = await db.execute("SELECT * FROM wallets")
    wallets = await wallets_cursor.fetchall()
    wallet_balances = []

    for w in wallets:
        funded_row = await (
            await db.execute(
                "SELECT COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0) as total FROM funding_events WHERE wallet_id = ?",
                (w["id"],),
            )
        ).fetchone()
        spent_row = await (
            await db.execute(
                "SELECT COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0) as total FROM transactions WHERE wallet_id = ?",
                (w["id"],),
            )
        ).fetchone()
        balance = funded_row["total"] - spent_row["total"]
        wallet_balances.append(
            {
                "wallet_id": w["id"],
                "name": w["name"],
                "type": w["type"],
                "balance": round(balance, 2),
            }
        )

    recent_cursor = await db.execute(
        "SELECT t.*, w.name as wallet_name FROM transactions t "
        "JOIN wallets w ON t.wallet_id = w.id "
        "ORDER BY t.date DESC, t.created_at DESC LIMIT 5"
    )
    recent = [dict(r) for r in await recent_cursor.fetchall()]

    return {
        "month": month,
        "total_spent": round(total_spent, 2),
        "daily_average": round(daily_avg, 2),
        "by_category": by_category,
        "wallet_balances": wallet_balances,
        "recent_transactions": recent,
    }

from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from typing import Optional
import csv, io
from app.database import get_db
from app.auth import verify_token

router = APIRouter(dependencies=[Depends(verify_token)])


@router.get("/api/export/csv")
async def export_csv(
    from_date: Optional[str] = None, to_date: Optional[str] = None, db=Depends(get_db)
):
    query = """
        SELECT t.date, t.description, t.category, t.payment_method,
               t.amount, w.name as wallet
        FROM transactions t
        JOIN wallets w ON t.wallet_id = w.id
        WHERE 1=1
    """
    params = []
    if from_date:
        query += " AND t.date >= ?"
        params.append(from_date)
    if to_date:
        query += " AND t.date <= ?"
        params.append(to_date)
    query += " ORDER BY t.date DESC"

    cursor = await db.execute(query, params)
    rows = await cursor.fetchall()

    output = io.StringIO()
    writer = csv.writer(output)
    writer.writerow(
        ["date", "description", "category", "payment_method", "amount", "wallet"]
    )
    for row in rows:
        writer.writerow(
            [
                row["date"],
                row["description"],
                row["category"],
                row["payment_method"],
                row["amount"],
                row["wallet"],
            ]
        )

    output.seek(0)
    return StreamingResponse(
        iter([output.getvalue()]),
        media_type="text/csv",
        headers={"Content-Disposition": "attachment; filename=paisa-export.csv"},
    )

@router.post("/api/wallets", status_code=201)

async def get_cycles(db=Depends(get_db)):
    wallets_cursor = await db.execute("SELECT * FROM wallets ORDER BY id")
    wallets = await wallets_cursor.fetchall()
    result = []

    for wallet in wallets:
        wid = wallet["id"]

        last_funding = await (
            await db.execute(
                "SELECT * FROM funding_events WHERE wallet_id = ? ORDER BY date DESC, id DESC LIMIT 1",
                (wid,),
            )
        ).fetchone()

        if not last_funding:
            result.append(
                {
                    "wallet_id": wid,
                    "wallet_name": wallet["name"],
                    "wallet_type": wallet["type"],
                    "funding_event_id": None,
                    "funded_on": None,
                    "opening_amount": 0,
                    "leftover_from_previous": 0.0,
                    "total_available": 0.0,
                    "total_spent": 0.0,
                    "current_balance": 0.0,
                    "transactions": [],
                }
            )
            continue

        prev_funding = await (
            await db.execute(
                "SELECT * FROM funding_events WHERE wallet_id = ? AND id < ? ORDER BY date DESC LIMIT 1",
                (wid, last_funding["id"]),
            )
        ).fetchone()

        leftover = 0.0
        if prev_funding:
            prev_spent_row = await (
                await db.execute(
                    "SELECT COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0) as total FROM transactions "
                    "WHERE wallet_id = ? AND date >= ? AND date < ?",
                    (wid, prev_funding["date"], last_funding["date"]),
                )
            ).fetchone()
            leftover = max(
                0, prev_funding["amount"] + leftover - prev_spent_row["total"]
            )

        total_available = last_funding["amount"] + leftover

        txs_cursor = await db.execute(
            "SELECT t.*, w.name as wallet_name FROM transactions t "
            "JOIN wallets w ON t.wallet_id = w.id "
            "WHERE t.wallet_id = ? AND t.date >= ? "
            "ORDER BY t.date DESC",
            (wid, last_funding["date"]),
        )
        txs = await txs_cursor.fetchall()
        total_spent = sum(tx["amount"] for tx in txs)

        result.append(
            {
                "wallet_id": wid,
                "wallet_name": wallet["name"],
                "wallet_type": wallet["type"],
                "funding_event_id": last_funding["id"],
                "funded_on": last_funding["date"],
                "opening_amount": last_funding["amount"],
                "leftover_from_previous": round(leftover, 2),
                "total_available": round(total_available, 2),
                "total_spent": round(total_spent, 2),
                "current_balance": round(total_available - total_spent, 2),
                "transactions": [dict(tx) for tx in txs],
            }
        )

    return result

# digit-rss-tracker - Setup Guide

Repository to track an author on digit and notify when he posts an article (made to track a goated friend named vyom ramani)

## What you're setting up

A Python script that runs daily on your Hetzner server, checks Vyom's RSS feed
on digit.in, and sends a push notification to your phone via ntfy when a new
article is posted.

The script validates the feed is reachable before doing anything, stores a list
of articles it's already notified you about, and only pings you for new ones.

---

## Before you start — what you need on your machine

You already ran test_feed.py locally and confirmed the feed works. Good.
Now you just need to SSH into your server. On Mac, Terminal is all you need —
it's built in, no extra software required.

---

## Step 1 — Phone setup (do this first)

1. Install the **ntfy** app on your phone:
   - Android: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=io.heckel.ntfy
   - iOS: https://apps.apple.com/app/ntfy/id1625396347

2. Open the app → tap the "+" button → enter a topic name
   - A topic is just your personal notification channel — like a secret radio
     frequency. Anyone who knows the name can subscribe, so make it hard to guess.
   - Good example: vyom-digit-ansh-7k3x2
   - Bad example: vyom or digit (too guessable)
   - Write it down — you'll need it in Step 4

---

## Step 2 — SSH into your server

Open Terminal on your Mac and run:

ssh root@YOUR_SERVER_IP

Replace YOUR_SERVER_IP with your Hetzner server's IP address.
You'll be dropped into a command prompt on your server.

---

## Step 3 — Create the project folder and add the script

Create a folder for the project:

mkdir -p ~/digit-rss-tracker
    cd ~/digit-rss-tracker

Now open a new file called checker.py in nano (a simple terminal text editor):

nano checker.py

Paste the full contents of checker.py here, then:

- Ctrl+O → Enter (saves the file)
- Ctrl+X (exits nano)

---

## Step 4 — Set your ntfy topic in the script

Open the script again:

nano checker.py

Find this line near the top:

NTFY_TOPIC = "YOUR_SECRET_TOPIC_HERE"

Change it to your actual topic name from Step 1, e.g.:

NTFY_TOPIC = "vyom-digit-ansh-7k3x2"

Save and exit (Ctrl+O → Enter → Ctrl+X).

---

## Step 5 — Install dependencies

Your server needs two Python libraries. Run these commands:

# Check Python 3 is available — should print something like 3.10.x or 3.11.x
    python3 --version

# Install pip (Python's package manager) if it's not already there
    sudo apt update && sudo apt install python3-pip -y

# Install the two libraries the script uses:
    # feedparser → reads and parses RSS feeds
    # requests   → makes HTTP calls (used for both feed fetching and ntfy notification)
    pip3 install feedparser requests --break-system-packages

The --break-system-packages flag is needed on newer Ubuntu versions — it just
tells pip it's okay to install into the system Python environment.

---

## Step 6 — Run the script manually to test it

cd ~/digit-rss-tracker
    python3 checker.py

Expected output on first run:

HTTP calls (used for both feed fetching and ntfy notification)
    pip3 install feedparser requests --break-system-packages

The --break-system-packages flag is needed on newer Ubuntu versions — it just
tells pip it's okay to install into the system Python environment.

---

## Step 6 — Run the script manually to test it

cd ~/digit-rss-tracker
    python3 checker.py

Expected output on first run:

─── Digit Article Checker ───
    [→] Validating feed: https://www.digit.in/author/vyomramani/feed/
    [✓] Feed is valid. Found 10 articles in feed.
    [✓] Notified: Sam Altman investigation: 6 crazy revelations
    [✓] Notified: Sam Altman to blame? Why Microsoft and OpenAI are drifting apart
    ... (one line per article)
    [✓] Done — 10 new article(s) notified.
    ─────────────────────────────

Your phone will buzz for all 10 current articles — that's completely expected.
The script is marking them all as "already seen" so on every future run it only
notifies you about genuinely new ones.

If the feed is unreachable for any reason you'll see:

[✗] Feed validation failed: Feed URL returned HTTP 404.
        No notifications sent. Will try again next run.

---

## Step 7 — Set up the daily cron job

Cron is Linux's built-in task scheduler. You write one line telling it when to
run your script, and it handles it automatically forever — even after reboots.

Open the cron editor:

crontab -e

If it asks which editor to use, pick nano (option 1).

Add this line at the very bottom of the file:

0 9 * * * /usr/bin/python3 /root/digit-rss-tracker/checker.py >> /root/digit-rss-tracker/checker.log 2>&1

Breaking down what each part means:

0 9 * * *       → when to run. Format is: minute | hour | day | month | weekday
                      0 9 * * * = at minute 0 of hour 9 = 9:00 AM, every day
    /usr/bin/python3          → full path to Python. Cron needs full paths, not shortcuts
    /root/digit-rss-tracker/checker.py → your script, also full path
    >> checker.log            → append all printed output to a log file
    2>&1                      → also capture any errors into the same log file

Save and exit (Ctrl+O → Enter → Ctrl+X).
Cron will confirm: "crontab: installing new crontab"

---

## Changing the schedule

Want to check every 2 days instead of daily?

0 9 */2 * *     → 9am every 2 days

Every 12 hours:

0 */12 * * *    → midnight and noon every day

---

## Checking the log anytime

To see what the script has been doing:

cat ~/digit-rss-tracker/checker.log

Each run appends to this file so you have a full history.

---

## Files on your server after setup

~/digit-rss-tracker/
    ├── checker.py          ← the main script
    ├── seen_articles.txt   ← auto-created on first run, one URL per line
    └── checker.log         ← auto-created by cron, full run history

---

## Updating the author or ntfy topic

To track a different author, open checker.py and change FEED_URL at the top.
To change your ntfy topic, change NTFY_TOPIC and update your phone subscription.
